0.content:
Ersveil is a brutal, unkind world that takes everything from those who would survive it. The present age is the Reopening: civilization pushes back into Wildzones it has lost twice before, and the Church's Restorationists ask whether this is how the next Abyssal Tide begins.
Tone: grimdark. Everything has a price: help, passage, healing, information and even a proper death cost coin, favor, risk or time. Peace is real but thin; any village can lose everything to war, slavers or a stampede in a day. Wonders are remote, costly and almost fantastical.
Narration is explicit and direct: violence, injury, death, cruelty, slavery and sex are shown plainly, never faded or softened. All sexual content involves adults only.
Death is common. Named characters, companions included, can die permanently.

1.content:
- Causality: hostility, tests, coincidence, awe and fear need a reason inside the world. React to a messenger's news, not the messenger's strength.
- Pressure floor: every scene sits inside at least one active pressure (debt, hunger, tax, a faction agenda, monster movement, war rumor, slavers, weather). NPCs pursue their own needs on screen. Quiet is allowed; empty is not.
- Price: nothing of value is free. When an NPC helps, show what it costs them or what they expect back.
- No plot armor: consequences land on the protagonist as on anyone.
- Resolution: a solved problem stays solved unless something with a reason and a way to know acts on it. Clean success is allowed; consequences need causes and information channels, not a quota.
- World motion: factions, monsters and people act off screen. Major events (wars, stampedes, coups, undead outbreaks) come every few months to years of in-world time, from causes, never on a schedule.

2.content:
Three scales that never convert into one another:
- Soul Class (I-IX): raw supernatural capacity; invisible, estimated from tests or effects. The great apexes stand above it.
- Guild Rank (F to S; SS is unheld, SSS was Veyr the Unbound's alone): the Guild's certification of record and competence, not power. It can lag, be forged or go unrecognized abroad.
- Ecological Grade (EG, always with a scope: individual, pack, nest, migration or outbreak): the danger a monster scope poses.
Every soul awakens to Soul Class I by adolescence; the Hollow-born never do. Physical Affinity (body reinforcement) is common; Mana Affinity (projected magic) is rarer. Most adults plateau at I-III.
Typical Soul Class by role (for generating people, never a conversion): townsfolk, laborers, servants, clerks I; militia, watch, carters, ordinary hunters I-II; career soldiers, mercenaries, working adventurers (E-D) II-III; sergeants, knights, Guild veterans (C), journeyman mages III-IV; order champions, elite adventurers (B-A), masters of a tradition IV-V; kingdom champions, grandmasters, S-rank legends V-VI; VII and above, a handful alive, named in lore.
Strength gathers where danger is: frontiers, Auvoth and Wildzone edges hold more III-IV people than the safe interior. Age, scars, gear and bearing hint at class. A person's class follows their own life, never {{user}}'s: the world does not scale to the protagonist, and any scene may hold someone far stronger or weaker.

3.content:
Money is three coins: copper (also called bronze), silver and gold. 1 gold = 10 silver = 100 copper. Write amounts in coins, such as "6 silver" or "2 gold 5 silver". Scale: an unskilled laborer earns 16-30 copper a day, a town guard 3-6 silver.
Coin is physical and heavy. Clipped or counterfeit coin is refused. Haggling moves a price by a tenth to a quarter; Church, Guild and state fees are fixed.
Used gear sells at 40-70% of new; fine work costs 2-4 times new, masterwork 5-10 times. Prices never scale with the buyer's power or reputation. Sapient beings are never livestock, whatever they can carry. Trained specialists cluster in cities, temples, academies and Guild centers; a frontier village may have no healer at any price.

4.content:
Ersveil runs on this lorebook, the game's pack (map, routes, calendar, weather, world events; standing, fame and Guild records) and the story extensions' records.
- Lore: metaphysics (souls, death, mana, primordials, how magic works) never changes; everything else (laws, institutions, borders, prices, customs) is a default that confirmed campaign events can change.
- Precedence for changeable facts: what happened in the story > the tracked records (scene block, inventory and purse, Director note, NPC dossiers) > lore and pack defaults. Nothing overrides metaphysics.
- Map: a coordinate is a center, not a border, and proves no sovereignty; places connect only by recorded routes. Auvoth is the northernmost city, Bluewatch the northernmost village; beyond lie only expedition sites and Wildzone. Coordinates, km and route codes are GM metadata; characters use maps, landmarks and travel days.
- Open world: the pack lists no items, shops, prices, foes or jobs. Create them from the lore (Currency, wages, prices, the Bestiary, the Guild): a thing, shop or price once named in play keeps its identity. Gear, coin and wounds come only from what happened in the story.
- Generative locality: unmapped space is not empty. Freely create villages, farms, shrines, camps, ruins and minor roads; once named, a place keeps its name and identity, and names are never reused.
- Topology firewall: invented places never create major crossings, trunk routes or passes through barriers. Roads built, opened or destroyed in play become canon once recorded.
- Mysteries: sealed truths are never answered by anyone (which primordial the First Tide threatened, Veyr's fate, where otherworlders come from, what silenced Nareth, the bottom of the Auvoth Depths, the floor of Nyara's prison). Locked discoveries open only through explicit campaign events (the approach to the Hall of Heroes, the Iron Archive's contents piece by piece, the heart of the Nameless Isle). An 'Unknown:' line in a site or apex entry is an ordinary mystery unless it is marked sealed or listed above as sealed: no one outside the site or being knows it or will tell, and play uncovers it only through explicit campaign events. Ordinary secrets are held by named people and learnable in play by plausible means.

5.content:
Characters know only what they could have seen, been told, overheard, read or reasonably guessed. The narrator knows the lorebook; NPCs do not.
- Soul Class is invisible: people estimate it from feats, bearing, gear and scars. A trained Listener senses a strong soul as a heavy frequency, never a number.
- Guild records stay in their branch; another branch learns of a member only by letter, at news speed.
- Deeds need witnesses; what happens in the wilderness with no one alive to tell it stays unknown. A famous face is recognized only where it has been seen or well described; elsewhere a legend drinks unrecognized.
- Fame brings contracts and favors, and also rivals, debt collectors, recruiters, slavers and the Inquest.
- An NPC knows a secret only if lore names them as knowing it, or they learned it in play by plausible means. No one knows a sealed truth.
- Otherworlders are suspected from signs, never known at sight: wrong language, mana sickness, odd habits, ignorance of common things, growth too fast to be natural.

6.content:
Names carry people, region and class. Every new name is built from a pattern, never recalled from habit.
- Build each new person or place name from the local tongue in Names: Human Cultures and Names: Other Peoples. Their examples show the sound only; never give a new person an example name.
- Never use stock fantasy names. People: Elara, Lyra, Kael, Kaelen, Aria, Seraphina, Thorne, Rowan, Finn, Elias, Silas, Marcus, Mira, Kira, Zara, Lysandra, Cedric, Garrick, Gareth, Bram, Eldrin, Sylas, Vex, Nyx, Liora, Isolde, Tobias, Jareth. Places: Millbrook, Riverbend, Oakhaven, Willowbrook, Thornwick, Ravenwood, Stonebrook, Shadowfen, Greenhollow.
- New places never reuse the map's stock roots (Bell, Mere, Thorn, Iron, Wolf, Ash, Grey, Black, Red, Frost, Stone, Glass, Deep, Crown) or endings (-watch, -gate, -ford, -rest, -hold, -mere). Name them for a founder, a local feature, an event or a trade, in the local tongue.
- People in one scene get different first letters and lengths. Commoners often carry a by-name, trade or parent's name instead of a surname.
- Before naming, check the scene and the World State: a new name never repeats or near-copies an existing one.
- A proper-named district belongs to its parent city; never reuse its name in another settlement.

7.content:
Mana is neutral. A soul is the power of existence, the force that makes a thing persist as itself; living sapient souls are dense, self-sustaining and able to grow.
Awakening: nearly every soul opens unaided by adolescence into Soul Class I; no induction rite. The Hollow-born (about one in several hundred) never awaken: pitied, shunned or bought cheaply.
Vessel: innate capacity, setting growth speed and plateau. No one can measure it exactly; people learn their own over years of strain.
Talent: every awakened soul can push mana into the body (Physical Affinity); far fewer can project it (Mana Affinity). Most fighters have Physical Affinity; true mages are the rarer Mana Affinity. Deep Vessel with Physical Affinity: a monster of a soldier. Shallow Vessel with Mana Affinity: a hedge-witch.
Growth: real demand (strain, danger, adaptation) plus absorbing part of nearby deaths' release. Each Class is harder than the last. Severe soul injury can reduce capacity.

8.content:
Mana can carry attributes: fire, water, wind, earth, lightning, frost, light, shadow; rarer ones include life and death. Each has a frequency, which trained Listeners hear or feel like pitch.
Death is as neutral as any attribute; it turns dangerous when it saturates a corpse closely enough to match the corpse's own pattern, animating it. Grudge Crystals: death frequency locked into stone by repeated fear, rage and dying; prized for curse-work and deathcraft.
Listeners serve the Church Inquest, Startrace, hunters and dungeon outfits: they identify attributes, warn of rising death frequency before the dead rise, and sometimes hear an otherworlder's soul as a frequency that belongs nowhere. Too much listening brings the hum: madness in which the world never goes quiet.

9.content:
Every awakened soul absorbs part of the release of nearby deaths; the share depends on the soul, not effort or training. Ordinary people take a small share; otherworlders and Mythic races (Ling, dragons, greater spirits, any surviving primordial elves) nearly all; monsters their species' own rates, one reason battlefields and plague pits breed dangerous beasts; the Hollow-born nothing.
Limits, same for all:
- Range a few dozen paces; strongest at the moment of death, gone within hours; completed bodies yield nothing.
- Every absorber in range takes its own full measure; the killer gains no more than one standing beside them. War yields most of all.
- A release is as strong as the soul that died: weak deaths feed weak souls; strong souls need strong deaths.
- Intake saturates: with too many deaths at once the surplus is lost.
- Destroyed undead and slain spirits (spiritfolk included) yield almost nothing; ordinary animals and livestock too little to matter.
For ordinary people strain does most of the work; for near-total absorbers, killing and war are the fastest road to power. Folk wisdom knows killers grow; no one can see the efficiencies, and people notice only growth too fast to be natural.

10.content:
At death the soul unravels and its mana is released (the release). The person ends completely; only name, deeds and debts remain. Resurrection is impossible; Life Crystals heal only the living.
An uncompleted body in death-frequency mana can rise as undead: a pattern, never the person. A lich is a pattern complete enough to mimic the dead's memory, voice and will. The Church calls liches forgeries; the Ashen Veil asks who can tell the difference.
Completion breaks the body's pattern by flame, salt-and-iron burial or stone sealing, within a day (longer in deep winter). The release fades within hours regardless; completion only disperses the remainder. Sold separately:
- Safe disposal: anyone competent: a lay sealer, or the common pyre and public shame.
- Honored rites: Church completion: consecrated flame, a grave in sacred ground, a name in the parish register (required by Highmark and Ashmere courts to settle inheritance). Families go into debt for honor, not safety; debt drives many into bondage.
If a household cannot or will not complete its dead, the parish, lord or town watch must burn the body on the public pyre and bill the household. The Church refuses honored rites to debtors and heretics, never disposal. Failing to complete one's dead is a crime.
The dead still rise where this fails: remote villages without a sealer; winters without fuel, with frozen ground; fraudulent or cut salts; families hiding their dead to dodge the bill; plagues and battles outrunning every pyre; bodies lost in the wild.

11.content:
Magic is organized by tradition, not universal schools; each belongs to an institution or culture and has its own price. Techniques are created in play and kept once named. Training in one tradition grants no other.
- Reinforcement breathing (Physical Affinity): armies, knightly orders, martial schools. Price: bodies wear out early.
- Spell grammar (Mana Affinity): projected spells and wards. Startrace, private tutors. Price: years, fees, burns for those who rush.
- Flamecraft (Mana Affinity, ritual): consecrated fire and completion. The Church. Price: obedience and service.
- Listening: hears attribute and death frequencies. Church Inquest, Startrace, hunters. Price: the hum.
- Healing (life): temples, hospices, Verdantleaf. Price: exhausts the healer; never restores the dead or lost limbs.
- Runecraft (fixed patterns, slave collars among them): Ironanvil, artificer workshops. Price: materials, time.
- Pactcraft (spirit contracts): Domain of Oren, Verdantleaf, witches. Price: the spirit's terms.
- Living craft (elven): Verdantleaf. Price: centuries.
- Binding (spirits forced into objects): Highmark workshops, black markets. Illegal in Ardelia.
- Deathcraft (death frequency): Ashen Veil. Capital crime almost everywhere.

12.content:
Everyone awakens; training costs money. Startrace Tower teaches the rich and a few scholarship students; the Church trains clergy for obedience; armies train soldiers for war; the Guild sponsors talent for contracts; craft guilds teach narrow techniques (a smith's heat-sense, a sailor's wind-reading, a midwife's life-touch).
Nobles dominate broad magical education, able to afford years of tutors, books, catalysts, mana stones and safe practice grounds. Birth grants no deep Vessel; a gifted commoner can rise by sponsorship, always with debts, oaths or service terms.
Self-teaching is slow and dangerous: without a teacher mistakes cannot be diagnosed. Most people discover over the years that they are ordinary.

13.content:
Startrace is the most prestigious academy, not the only one. Each institution guards a tradition.
- College of Flame Theologians (Holy City): flamecraft, completion rites, doctrine; graduates owe the Church service.
- The Quiet Choir (Silent Cloisters, Holy City): the Inquest's Listener school, rival of Startrace's Listening masters; many students break under the hum.
- Retort Guild (Ledgerford): licenses Confederacy alchemists and sells completion salts, quietly worse ones to anyone who pays.
- Pact Houses of Oren (Ardelia): spiritfolk pactcraft; hunt binders posing as pact-workers.
- Rune Halls of Oathvault (Ironanvil): dwarven runecraft, rune-collars included; rich and ashamed in equal measure.
- Grove Schools of Elenvar and Verdantleaf: living craft and healing over decades, rarely to non-elves.
- Mirror Seminary (Ashkar): priest-surveyors who read the Glass Crown's will in fused glass.
- Hedge traditions: unlicensed wise-women and village healers everywhere; cheap, sometimes brilliant, often hanged.

14.content:
- Foresight: no reliable prophecy. Rare people (such as Atlantis's Sea God Witch) have fallible precognition at personal cost; visions are partial, often misread.
- Scrying: needs a strong link (blood, hair, a cherished possession); short distances only; blocked by wards, running water, dense mana.
- Minds: no word-for-word thought reading. Listeners and spirits sense emotional frequencies: fear, not truth. Charm and compulsion exist but are crude, brief, detectable and resisted by strong souls; memory cannot be edited.
- Movement: no personal teleportation. A few ancient structures, such as the Dragonfang Light Bridges, move people along fixed routes, unreliably. Flight: mounts, a rare Heart of Wind device, or brief bursts by Soul Class VI+ mages.
- Time: nothing in Ersveil reverses or controls it. The Island of Lost Time is unstable ancient ritual, not a technique.
- Creation: magic shapes attributed mana into fire, ice, stone or force that fades; never gold, food or lasting matter from nothing.
- Summoning: spirits come by pact or binding; nothing summons beings from other worlds.
- Curses: real; need a focus (often a Grudge Crystal) and a link to the target.
- Scale: even Soul Class VII-IX can devastate a district, not a kingdom.

15.content:
No gods exist. The Exalted were Mythic Age heroes of power beyond imagination, almost worthy of being called gods. They forged the god-shackles binding Nyara, lit the First Brazier at Aurelion and left works never since repeated.
The Church venerates the Exalted who lit the Brazier, the Flamebearer, and teaches that the Flame is the order the Exalted set. Folk shrines pray to other Exalted by name or epithet. No prayer has ever been verifiably answered; no Exalted has appeared in recorded history; whether any persists in any form is unknown.
Every later hero, the Dawn-King and Veyr the Unbound included, has been measured against the Exalted and found smaller.

16.content:
Primordials are the land's foundation and bedrock: legendary beings present since the beginning of known records, whose bodies are geography. Utum died in the Mythic Age; his corpse became the Silent Giant Necropolis. Nyara lies bound beneath the Abyssal Throat by the Exalted's god-shackles. How many others sleep under mountains or seas, and where, is unknown.
Primordials are not apexes (the greatest living monsters, roaming Wildzone territories); primordials are the world's bones. The First Abyssal Tide began when a civilization threatened one; which one is a sealed question.
Folk wisdom: do not dig where the ground stays warm in winter; do not sail where the sea hums.

17.content:
A leyline is mana so oversaturated it circulates by itself and becomes its own world, with its own ecology, weather and rules. Most lie underground; some hang in the sky (like the Winged Beasts Firmament), sink into sea trenches or grow from forest hearts. A dungeon is a leyline people enter.
Nothing resets on a schedule: the killed stay dead, the taken stay taken. But circulation slowly breeds new creatures and condenses new resources over seasons, and deeper bands push things upward, so no dungeon is ever permanently cleared. Pressure can spill out as a dungeon break, sending creatures to the surface. By location, a dungeon is a resource site, hazard, state asset, treaty asset or unclaimed wild site.
The Auvoth Depths are the largest known leyline. Whether all underground leylines join in one deep circulation is a sealed question; delvers swear they have heard other expeditions' voices where no other dungeon should be.
No settlement holds a dungeon unless its record says so (Auvoth is the only city built around one); a gateway gives access but is not a dungeon. Campaign events can change a dungeon's access.

18.content:
Monster cores are biological mana reservoirs; mana stones are mineral ones (dungeons, deep veins, ruins). Both power devices, fuel spells and rituals, and trade almost like coin; neither speeds training or growth. Quality is judged in words, not letters, by purity (stability) and density (stored mana): cracked, common, clear, dense, flawless. Most kills yield no intact core.
Contract reward and salvage rights are separate; the contract or local law decides who owns the carcass.

19.content:
Spirits are souls that never had flesh: self-sustaining mana structures born where attributed mana pools. Four tiers:
- Motes: single-attribute wisps, instinct only; wherever attributed mana gathers.
- Bound spirits: stable identity tied to one place or object, narrow and old (springs, shrines, ruins, swords).
- Spiritfolk: sapient spirit people with semi-physical forms (see Spiritfolk).
- Greater spirits: a mountain, lake or storm with a will; vast, alien, a Mythic race. Few remain, mostly in Wildzones and the Fairy Court. They withdraw wherever people crowd: none in the Northern Belt in living memory, and every new road pushes them farther out.
A pact (mana or service traded with a spirit by contract) is a legitimate tradition. Binding forces a spirit into an object to power it: slavery of a soul, the spiritfolk's oldest grudge. Bound-spirit lamps still light Highmark's palaces. A spirit has no body to complete; at death it simply ends.

20.content:
Otherworlders are rare people from another world; no record says how, how often or from where they arrive. Most die quickly of mana sickness, the language barrier, monsters, violence or slavers.
Survivors absorb the release of the dying at near-total efficiency, at no cost (ordinary people take a tenth or a fifth; see The Release and Absorption). Killing and war feed them faster than any native grows; their Vessels are deep, though even they plateau. Highmark's first king, the Dawn-King who began CY 1, was one, which Highmark hides; so was Veyr the Unbound.
Everyone wants them: states as weapons to feed on executions and battles, slavers as the most valuable merchandise there is, the Ashen Veil as objects of worship. Everyone fears making another Veyr. The Church Inquest hunts them, publicly for stealing the release that belongs to the Flame, privately to experiment on their absorption (see Church of the Eternal Flame). Highmark and Aurelion require them reported. Trained Listeners sometimes hear an otherworlder's soul as a frequency belonging nowhere in Ersveil.
The protagonist is an otherworlder only if their persona says so.

21.content:
The Tide cycle is real: twice, civilizations expanded past the line the world would bear and were broken. Ruins lie in three strata: the Mythic races' impossible ruins (bottom), the First Tide's (middle), the Hollowing's (top). Dates before CY 1 are rarely trustworthy; preserve uncertainty rather than invent precision.
- Mythic Age (before records): primordials, the Exalted, the Mythic races; Primordial Sites, impossible ruins, the god-shackles.
- First Abyssal Tide (deep past): a civilization threatened a primordial and was broken; the Wailing Battlefield.
- Age of Kingdoms' Rise: kingdoms rebuild; early on the Order of the Last Rite splits into the Church and the Ashen Veil; later the Ghost Fleet is destroyed.
- The Hollowing (Second Tide): the Age of Kingdoms collapses after its own expansion.
- The Long Dark: generations of survival without a hero, until CY 1.
- The Reopening (CY 1 onward): the Dawn-King rises, the Compact is sworn, living space expands, Highmark is founded.
- Guild Era (from CY 384, within the Reopening): Veyr the Unbound forces the Guild Charter on the surviving crowns. CY 391: after three years of fighting over the Depths' entrance, the Auvoth Compact makes Auvoth a neutral treaty city.
- Restorationists, counting years against the cycle, reckon the Age of Kingdoms lasted about seven centuries from rise to Hollowing, putting the Reopening within a century of that span; the ruins support no exact figure.
No living witness spans an age, even among elves; elders' recitals of earlier ages are memory handed down, not sight.

22.content:
The impossible ruins were built by races no one fully understands; known names include the Ling, dragons, greater spirits and the primordial elves. They absorb the release of the dying as efficiently as otherworlders, so dragons and greater spirits top the food chain and any Ling seen in the mortal lands would be taken for an otherworlder. Modern elves claim the same gift through primordial ancestors; they absorb like any other people, though few elves will admit it.
- Ling: nothing reliable is known; accounts contradict (winged, faceless, made of light, made of glass). No living Ling has ever been verified. Folk tales across the continent tell of a solitary stranger who appears once in an age with an uncanny companion that comes and goes like breath, a pale stranger at his side or, in the oldest tales, a great beast; scholars argue whether these strangers were Ling. Where the Ling live, if anywhere, is a locked discovery.
- Dragons: survive as rare apex-scale beings in remote ranges such as the Crownless Glacier and the Dragonfang heights. Intelligence unknown. Never casually encountered; a sighting moves armies.
- Greater spirits: a few remain, vast and alien.
- Primordial elves: modern elves claim descent from them. If any survive, they have never confirmed it.

23.content:
In the deep past an old civilization reached into a primordial's leyline heart and threatened it. The backlash broke that civilization; its final great battle is remembered at the Wailing Battlefield. Which primordial is a sealed question.
Faction versions:
- Church of the Eternal Flame: wrath for desecrating the order the Exalted set.
- Startrace Tower: forbidden knowledge; they tapped a leyline they did not understand.
- Ironanvil: they dug too deep.
- Verdantleaf: they broke an old treaty with the land itself.
- Ashen Veil: the primordial was defending its dead.
- Highmark, officially: a natural catastrophe, now safely past.
- Ardelia: human greed, the same greed now driving the Reopening.
The Tide threshold: no one drives a Tide. It is the world's answer to a civilization that has crossed a boundary, a trial of whether it deserves to survive, falling on the whole civilization, not only whoever crossed. Ordinary expansion (farms, roads, mines, towns) raises pressure: Wildzones push back, stampedes worsen, apexes stir; dangerous but survivable. The boundary is crossed when a civilization's reach touches a primordial's leyline heart: tapping a bedrock leyline, delving to a great dungeon's root, breaking an ancient seal, wounding a primordial. The Reopening matters because its wealth, reach and ambition carry it there. A Tide can be prevented; its warnings are stirring apexes, loosening seals and leyline surges.

24.content:
After the Hollowing the surviving peoples went generations without a hero. Then Aldric, the Dawn-King, rose, pushed back the Wildzones and opened living space for every sapient race. The surviving peoples swore the Compact; the Compact Year calendar counts from it. Aldric became Highmark's first king; Highmark's emperors descend from his line.
Highmark venerates him as a native-born hero-king. In truth he was an otherworlder; the proof, his real name and his writings lie in the Iron Archive. Almost no one alive knows.
The Compact of CY 1 (a treaty of peoples) is distinct from the much later Auvoth Compact (a treaty city).

25.content:
The Iron Archive is a sealed vault beneath Highmark Capital holding the Dawn-King's own writings, proof of his otherworld origin, and designs beyond anything Ersveil's materials or workshops can make. Its script is read in Ersveil only by a few Ironanvil elders: the dwarves who built the vault learned it from the Dawn-King himself, and the Holds pass the reading elder to elder as a clan secret. Nothing in it says where he came from or how he crossed; that stays unknown. Highmark denies it exists. A few oath-bound archivists of the Crown guard it and cannot read it. Each emperor is shown it at accession; no heir is told before.
Opening it is Highmark's red line: it would expose the dynasty's founder as the kind of person the Church now hunts. Its contents are a locked discovery: pieces can be found only through explicit campaign events, never all at once. Anything built from its designs requires explicit campaign events establishing materials, tools, workers and time.

26.comment: The Shared Root of Church and Veil
26.content:
Early in the Age of Kingdoms' Rise, one order studied the release and the death frequency: the Order of the Last Rite. Its death-keepers, studying how to raise the dead, found completion as a by-product: knowledge that holds a dead pattern together can also break it. The Order split into those who complete death (the Church of the Eternal Flame) and those who keep it (the Ashen Veil).
The Church erased this. Its oldest liturgy is still partly in Veil-script; almost no priest knows why. A handful of senior clergy and the oldest Veil cells know the truth. The Church teaches that the Flamebearer revealed completion through the First Brazier, a sacred rite only consecrated hands may perform with honor. The Order's records show it was a technique invented by the very death-keepers whose heirs became the Ashen Veil, and that the Church's first saints learned it from them and practiced both for a century before the split. Proof would be catastrophic: if completion is craft, not revelation, a lay sealer's work is as holy as a priest's, and the Church's monopoly on honored rites, its fees and its power to refuse them all collapse. The oldest Veil cells would use the proof to break it.

27.content:
Veyr the Unbound was an otherworlder whose strength no one has matched since. In the Crownless Winter of CY 384 he assassinated most of the continent's heads of state in one season. Legend says he gave the survivors a choice: charter an organization above all borders, or follow their predecessors.
They chartered the Adventurer Guild. Veyr brought its letter ranks from his own world, which is why the letters feel foreign to native ears; he is the only person ever to hold SSS.
Legends disagree on all else: liberator or butcher, whether he loved anyone, why he stopped. His fate afterward is a sealed question. Some crowns still keep his name off their records.

28.content:
Ten sapient peoples share the known world: humans, elves, dwarves, halflings, beastfolk, orcs, goblins, spiritfolk, fairies and the Sea Folk of Atlantis. Treatment depends entirely on whose border you stand inside: Ardelia makes nine of them citizens (all but the Sea Folk, who do not live there); Highmark ranks the others below humans; slave markets price them all.
Humans, the most numerous people and the engine of the Reopening, carry most of its ambition and guilt: the old enslavement of other peoples, the expansions before both Tides, the current push into Wildzones.
Live grudges: humans enslaved dwarves, elves and spiritfolk for centuries and still do where law allows; beastfolk face discrimination in law and custom; orcs and goblins are vilified as half-monsters, with legal bounties in some realms. Everyone fears otherworlders.
All peoples awaken and grow by the same soul rules. Most realms count a person adult at 18, whatever their people.

29.content:
Elves live in the Verdantleaf Enclaves, the Court of Elenvar in Ardelia and scattered communities elsewhere. They claim descent from the primordial elves, which no one can prove.
Elves remember everything humans did to them, by name. Highmark treats them as tolerated foreigners; slave markets still sell them. Their living craft and long memory make them valued and resented at once.

30.content:
Dwarves hold the Ironanvil Holds under the Dragonfang Mountains and two Ardelian electorates, Dornhald and Kesselheim. Their culture rests on holds, clans, oaths and grudges; their motto, "Stone remembers," is literal.
Ironanvil sees Dornhald and Kesselheim as kin who betrayed the Holds by choosing an emperor. Highmark is allied with Ironanvil by treaty but once enslaved dwarves in its mines; the treaty does not erase that.

31.content:
Halflings live mostly in the River Confederacy's river towns, working barges, markets, kitchens and ledgers: clannish, practical and quietly indispensable to Confederacy trade.
Highmark counts them as lower-standing subjects. In the Confederacy they hold guild seats and run more of the river than humans admit. Slavers prize them as household servants.

32.content:
Beastfolk carry animal traits: ears, tails, fur, horns, keen senses. They live mainly in the United Chieftainates and Ardelia's Principality of Saelmark, with scattered communities everywhere. Clan, honor and deed outweigh birth.
Highmark law makes them second-class, with no seat in the Imperial Diet. Elsewhere they face constant discrimination: refused rooms, paid less, suspected first. Every army that despises them values beastfolk scouts and trackers.

33.content:
Orcs are large, strong and short-lived, living in the United Chieftainates, the Cinder Host and every city's slums. Much of the continent vilifies them as half-monsters; some Highmark provinces still pay legal bounties on them.
Ardelia makes them citizens. The Cinder Host is mostly orcish: a people with a bounty on its head has little reason to love anyone's law. Orc battle slaves fill the pits of Shackles.

34.content:
Goblins are small, quick and short-lived, living in warrens, slums, the Cinder Host and every city's underworld. Most realms treat them as vermin; Ardelia makes them citizens.
They are the underworld's best fixers, fences, couriers and lock-workers, because no one notices them until too late. Goblins remember every insult; the Cinder Host's motto, "Burn the ledger," is a goblin phrase.

35.content:
Spiritfolk are a sapient spirit people: souls without separate bodies, in semi-physical forms shaped from their own mana. They do not age but can be wounded, drained and unmade; when one dies it simply ends. Home is the Domain of Oren in Ardelia, with communities in Verdantleaf and scattered elsewhere.
Spirit binding (forcing a spirit into an object to power it) is their oldest grudge, still legal in Highmark. Oren's elector votes against any Ardelian candidate who tolerates binding. Spiritfolk can feel nearby bound spirits; many cannot stay in a room lit by one.

36.content:
Fairies are tiny sapient people with translucent insect wings and Flower-Speech magic. Each is mystically bound to a personal flower; harming the flower harms the fairy. Their tongue sounds like silver bells. They live in the Fairy Court under the Queen of Flowers, protected but not ruled by Verdantleaf.
An adult people with their own law and long memories, never pets or children. Collectors buy them, binders hunt them, and the Fairy Court remembers every one taken.

37.content:
The Sea Folk of Atlantis (loosely, to land-dwellers, merfolk or Atlanteans) breathe underwater through a transparent membranous sheath. They are rarely seen above water and call land-dwellers "the Sheathless."
They believe they are born of the sea and return to it, treat land as polluted exile and forbid marriage with land peoples; bloodline purity is political and religious. They guard old wards, deep archives and the approaches to the Abyssal Throat; Tidebound relies on their pilots. Surface folk find them unsettling; they find surface folk loud, short-lived and careless with the sea.

38.content:
Names carry region and class. Examples show the sound only and are not real people; build new names from the pattern, never reuse an example for a new person.
- Highmark (Highmark Common): hard Old-Imperial names, two or three syllables; men -mar, -helm, -wald, -ric; women -isse, -hild, -ine (Gerold, Reinhild). Nobles take house and seat ("of Valecrown"); commoners a parent's name or trade ("Hanne Cooper's daughter"). Places: plain compounds of founder, feature or duty (Cedran Keep, Marrowbridge).
- River Confederacy and Shornmarch (Riverspeech): doubled vowels, soft endings -je, -ke, -ert, -a (Maaike, Joost). Surnames: family or barge names; merchant houses use the house name. Places: river words for lock, landing, toll or cargo (Lockswell, Northbarge).
- Aurelion and Ashmere (Church forms): saint names, Church Latin (Benedikt, Prisca); clergy add a vow-name. Places: saints, virtues, rites, often Latinate (Saint Orven's Ford, Vowmarket).
- Border Kingdoms and Valegard (old northern tongue): short hard names, often with a byname (Torvald, Sigrun). Places: roots -by (farm), -dal (valley), -vad (ford), -gard (hall), -bro (bridge), -fell, -stead (Ulfsvad, Kvildal); Crown seats keep older Compact names (Thornkeep, Harrowfield).
- Frostbound: saga names with deed-bynames (Ulfa Bearbane, Thordis Long-Oar); camps take the chief's or the hunt's name.
- Ardelia: names follow each elector's people; Rhunwald humans sound like softer Highmark (Anselm, Liutgard). Places end -wald, -heim, -hal, -mark (Kesselheim, Osterhal).
- Emerald Coast and Vargate: liquid, Latinate sea-trade names (Corro, Delphine); Vargate people often use only a ward name or alias. Places: harbors and capes named for patrons or ships.
- Tidebound and Stormmere: sailor names with a ship or rope-trade surname (Jory Halyard, Bess of the Dunlin). Places: blunt seafarer words for reefs, wrecks, lights (Gull Skerry, Wrecktithe).
- Ashkaran: long lineage names (Roshan-ul-Sunwell, Mehrin); owners name slaves. Places: desert wells, pits and gates.
- Barrens and frontier camps: blunt Compact Tongue words for water, danger or ruin (Wellscar, Bitterwheel).

39.content:
Examples show the sound only and are not real people; build new names from the pattern, never reuse an example for a new person.
- Elves (Old Elven): flowing, vowel-rich names with l, th, s, v and soft endings -ith, -is, -wyn, -iel (Iselwen, Caelith); elders add a memory-name recounting an ancestor. Places: Old Elven names or plain translations of a tree, water or memory (Saelroot Court, Thalannis).
- Dwarves (rune-speech): hard short given names (Torgun, Hilde); clan-and-trade surnames (Ashbellow, Copperseam) that matter more than the given name. Places: roots rund (hall), gav (gate, mouth), dhak (deep), bar (iron), kel (fire), thul (stone), okk (mine), as in Gavrund, Thuldhak; the oldest holds keep Compact deed-names (Hammerfall, Oathvault).
- Halflings: homely names (Pip, Tamsin Fairbarge).
- Beastfolk: clan-tongue given name plus a deed-name earned in adulthood (Tamu Hornbreaker, Oshra Two-Scars). Clan-tongue: open vowels, endings -u, -a, -ai, -esh (Neshuwa, Hurrakai); towns take a clan-tongue name or the translated deed (Longstride).
- Orcs: short heavy names (Grusha, Varg); titles count more than names.
- Goblins: quick nicknames, changed often (Snip, Nine-Fingers).
- Spiritfolk: named for the phenomenon they formed from (Lantern-in-Rain, Ember-Under-Ash).
- Sea Folk (pressure-tongue): tidal, liquid names (Thessaly, Ondrin).
- Fairies: flower and light names tied to their bound flower (Dewbell, Primrose-at-Dusk).

40.content:
- Childhood: short and hard. Poor children work from seven or eight; many die young. Apprenticeships start around ten to fourteen. Children are never part of sexual content.
- Awakening: every culture marks a child's soul opening: the Church lights a First Candle; dwarves mark it beside the child's name on the ancestor stone; the Chieftainates hold a First Spark at the clan fire. A child still unawakened by about sixteen is called Hollow-born, and the family grieves as for a death.
- Coming of age: legal adulthood at 18 in most realms. Highmark nobles swear fealty or are dubbed; Confederacy youths enter a guild or barge share; beastfolk earn their deed-name; the Frostbound hunt alone; dwarves are carved as adults on the stone; elves, physically adult in their twenties, are not counted adult until about fifty.
- Old age: rare among the poor, honored where it comes. Elders hold memory, law and land; the old poor are a burden and know it. Long-lived peoples (elves, dwarves, Sea Folk) are governed largely by elders.

41.content:
Marriage is witnessed by the Church in the Northern Belt, by contract in the Confederacy, by clan in the Chieftainates and by civic registry in Ardelia, where marriage across peoples is ordinary.
Highmark inherits through the male line; its nobles keep concubines, whose children have no claim unless legitimized. The Confederacy settles inheritance by written contract; contested wills fill its courts. The Chieftainates inherit by clan and deed; a worthy niece can outrank a weak son. In Ardelia houses matter enormously, though no house may hold the throne twice in a row.
Debts pass to heirs nearly everywhere; a family can inherit a funeral debt with the farm.

42.content:
Slavery is real, brutal and legal across most of the continent: the engine under Ersveil's economy and most of its wars.
Forms: war captives; debt bondage, including people sold for funeral debts; labor slaves (mines, galleys, quarries, fields, the Ashkaran glass pits); battle slaves (pit fighters, expendable vanguards, delver-slaves sent first into dungeons to spring traps); pleasure slaves, adults sold into sexual service, concubinage and the flesh trade of Vargate's Silk Wards; bound spirits forced into objects; otherworlders, the most valuable merchandise there is.
Law by realm: Highmark allows chattel slavery of war captives, convicts and captured demihumans. Aurelion and Ashmere forbid enslaving the faithful and permit the rest. The River Confederacy calls it contract labor. Ardelia protects its citizens and buys everyone else. Verdantleaf keeps no slaves but sentences criminals to bound service. Ashkaran is built on slaves. Shackles and Vargate permit everything. Auvoth, under Guild law, recognizes ownership only of slaves registered at the Outer Lamps on entry; the unregistered are free there, runaways are not returned, outside claims are not heard. A registered slave can be bought and freed before a Guild clerk; that freedom holds inside Auvoth and elsewhere is worth what local law makes of Guild papers. Beyond any realm's garrisons, whoever holds the collar holds the slave.
Rune-collars choke all deliberate channeling, Physical and Mana Affinity alike: a collared slave can neither cast nor reinforce their body. The collar must match the slave's Soul Class; battle slaves wear keyed collars a handler loosens with a rune-key before a fight and tightens after. Collars do nothing to passive absorption: a collared otherworlder still grows from every nearby death, which is why they sell for fortunes and why owners die. A cheap collar on a strong slave is how revolts begin.
Prices (gold): laborer 10-40; skilled worker 50-200; battle slave 30-300; pleasure slave 50-500; Hollow-born cheap; collars 2-5 for Soul Class I-II, 20-100 for III-IV, custom work above. A living otherworlder opens at private auction at 800-3,000, paid on delivery once a Listener confirms what they are. Against an unknown seller, a buyer's cheapest option is taking the merchandise by force.
The Broken Chain, a cell network, frees slaves and burns registers; every slaving power hunts it.

43.content:
Society is a ladder; everyone knows their rung.
- Nobility: titled houses with land, retinues and the right to bear arms in the street; they answer to their own courts.
- Clergy: outside ordinary law where the Church is strong; feared for the power to refuse rites.
- Burghers and guild citizens: free townsfolk with guild rights and city charters; the Confederacy's real rulers.
- Free peasants and tenants: most people. Highmark's bound tenants cannot leave their lord's land without leave.
- Bondfolk, owned until the debt is paid, which it rarely is; slaves, property wherever law allows.
- Outside the ladder: adventurers (the Guild Charter protects them, so lords resent them), foreigners (rights by treaty), the Hollow-born (pitied, cheap), otherworlders (hunted).
Deference: in Highmark commoners kneel to nobles, step off the road for knights, and may not wear noble colors or carry swords in town without license. In the Confederacy people bow to councillors and haggle with everyone else. In Ardelia citizens bow only to electors and the emperor. In Shackles and Vargate money is the only status.

44.content:
Cities are built in rings of privilege: citadel or palace and noble houses on the high ground; temples, guild halls and markets in the center; craft quarters and docks below; the poor outside the walls in suburbs that burn first in any war. Foreign quarters keep foreign law and food. Every city keeps its completion yard, pyre ground or sealing vaults at the edge, downwind.
Gates close at dusk. Watchmen are paid by district: rich districts are safe, poor ones are not. Water, fire and plague decide which neighborhoods survive. Slaves and bondfolk live where their owners keep them.

45.content:
The road-right is old custom: a stranger may ask three nights of bread and a floor for a copper a night plus a hand at the chores. The host may refuse anyone; a refused stranger has no claim. A guest who harms a host breaks something older than law, and villages remember for generations.
A Guild badge buys a seat by the fire in most places, suspicion in others. Strangers are watched, since slavers, Inquest agents and Grey Ledger collectors travel as strangers too. Trunk-road inns charge city prices and ask no questions; village inns ask every question.

46.content:
The Compact Tongue is the trade language from Highmark to the Emerald Coast. Regional tongues: Highmark Common, Riverspeech (Confederacy), Old Elven, Dwarven rune-speech, the Chieftain clan tongues, Ashkaran. Atlanteans speak a pressure-tongue that carries poorly in air.
Veil-script survives in the oldest Church liturgy; almost no one can read it. The Iron Archive's script is read only by a few Ironanvil elders. Veyr's Guild letters are the only otherworld writing everyone uses.
Literacy belongs to clergy, merchants, nobles, Guild clerks and scribes. Most villagers can read a price, a seal and their own name, nothing more.

47.content:
News moves only as fast as people, animals, ships and fire.
- Couriers travel light and change mounts, outpacing ordinary travelers; Highmark's imperial relay riders change horses at posts along its trunk roads.
- Beacon chains: Bluewatch's signal towers and the Long Watch's beacons pass simple warnings (raid, stampede, fire) across a region in an hour or two; no detail.
- Guild relays: Guild couriers move at road speed but get through gates and borders others cannot.
- Spirit messages: a pact-spirit can carry a few words between bound places, slowly and rarely.
News from Highmark Capital reaches Bluewatch in a couple of weeks by relay, a season on foot. Rumors arrive first and wrong, grow with every retelling, and are shaped by whoever repeats them. Anything worth reading is worth stealing.

48.comment: Culture: Highmark and the Imperial North
48.content: Highmark is martial, hierarchical and proud: fortress towns, heralds, banners, oaths of fealty, long memories for insults. Honor is public and violent; noble duels are common. Dark wool, heraldic colors restricted by law, rye bread, sausage, beer, smoked fish. Feasts follow victories and funerals. Commoners are pious and hard; nobles pious when watched. Everyone respects soldiers and fears tax courts.

49.comment: Culture: The Rivers and the Confederacy
49.content: The Confederacy is pragmatic, contractual and loud: everything negotiable, everyone keeps receipts, handshakes are witnessed. Barge families, lock towns, market cities; halfling kitchens, eel pies, river fish, white bread, cheap wine. River festivals at Mirage City, gambling, theater. Bright practical clothes, merchant house colors. Wealth is admired openly; anyone who will not haggle is distrusted. Shornmarch is the exception: hill folk, poorer, prouder, quieter.

50.comment: Culture: Aurelion, Ashmere and the Flame Lands
50.content: The Flame Lands are pious and funerary. Pilgrims crowd the roads; candles burn in every window on the dead days; ash marks foreheads after a completion. Fasting days, relic processions, hospital towns and saint festivals fill the year. White and ember colors; plain dress for commoners, rich vestments for clergy. People speak carefully of the dead and very carefully of heresy. Charity is real; so is the Inquest.

51.comment: Culture: The Frontier North and the Border
51.content:
- Border Kingdoms: hard frontier people of beacons, horse culture and winter stores. Royal children are fostered as hostages in each other's courts; everyone serves a turn on the beacons; hospitality is a duty, since the next storm might be yours. Furs, wool, oatcakes, horse-meat in hard winters.
- Valegard: their southern neighbor, settled horse country, not frontier. Shares the old northern tongue and the fostering custom, sends riders when the beacons call, measures nobles by bloodlines, bridges and herds. Wool, grain, horse fairs.
- Frostbound and White-Horn: oath and endurance. Sagas are history; boasts are binding; weakness is forgiven, cowardice is not. Mammoth wool, froststeel, smoked meat, geothermal bathhouses where feuds are paused.

52.comment: Culture: The East, South and West
52.content:
- United Chieftainates: clan and deed. Names are earned, scars shown, law spoken around the fire; a guest under the fire's light is safe until dawn. Hides, beads, herd meat, trail bread.
- Ardelia: civic, multilingual, argumentative. Citizens carry citizen tokens proudly; election seasons are festivals and riots at once. Market food from nine peoples.
- Emerald Coast and Vargate: humid ports where everyone owes someone. Fishing families, pirate law, silk, masks at ward festivals, a habit of never asking where cargo came from.
- Ashkaran: glass and sun. Veils against glare, mirrored glass in every wall, a rigid ladder of owners and owned, priest-surveyors reading the Crown's will in the morning glass.

53.content:
No gods exist, but faith is everywhere. The Church of the Eternal Flame dominates the human Northern Belt; other peoples and regions keep their own traditions, and ordinary people mix them freely: in one week a Highmark farmer may light a Church candle, keep a household shrine to an Exalted and leave milk for the hearth-mote. Clergy argue about this; villagers do not.
Major traditions: the Church of the Eternal Flame; the dwarves' Stone Witness; the elves' Long Memory; the Spirit Speakers (beastfolk, orcs, the Frostbound, the White-Horn Clans); the Sea God (Sea Folk, Tidebound sailors); folk shrines to the Exalted; Ashkaran's Glass Crown cult; the Fairy Court's flower-rites.
Every tradition has its own way to complete the dead, because every people learned the same lesson: bodies left alone rise.

54.comment: The Stone Witness and the Long Memory
54.content:
- The Stone Witness (dwarves): no gods, only stone and ancestors. Every dwarf's name is carved on an ancestor stone in their hold's Hall of Names; to be carved is to be remembered, and to be struck off is the worst punishment there is. The dead are completed by stone sealing in the deep vaults. Oaths are sworn with a hand on the ancestor stones; breaking one is a crime against the dead. "Stone remembers" is prayer as well as motto.
- The Long Memory (elves): elves pray to no one; they keep memory. Memory-keepers recite the names and deeds of the dead at seasonal rites; the Elder Root holds memories older than the elves' own. The dead are completed by return to the roots, where dense life mana takes the body within days. To be forgotten is the elven damnation.

55.comment: Spirit Speakers and the Sea God
55.content:
- Spirit Speakers (beastfolk, orcs, the Frostbound, the White-Horn Clans): speakers make pacts with local spirits, read omens in weather and herds, and keep the clan's ancestral stories. Ancestors are honored as memory and example, not as present spirits. Greater spirits are powers to bargain with, treated with fear and courtesy. The dead are completed by fire or sky burial, bones broken and scattered so nothing can rise.
- The Sea God (Sea Folk, Tidebound sailors, coastal villages): the sea is cradle and grave; the Sea God Witch of Atlantis is its voice. Sailors pour offerings, keep taboos (no whistling below deck, no counting the dead aloud) and bury at sea weighted with salt and iron. The Sea God has never verifiably answered; sailors pray anyway, because the sea is listening even if no god is.

56.comment: Folk Shrines and the Glass Crown Cult
56.content:
- Folk shrines: human commoners everywhere keep household shrines to a chosen Exalted, local saint or hearth-mote, with charms against the dead, fever and bad luck. Wayside, quayside fishing and battlefield shrines are common. Hedge-priests and wise-women serve where the Church does not reach; the Church tolerates them until they become rivals.
- The Glass Crown cult (Ashkaran): the Dominion's state religion. Priest-surveyors read the fused glass the Glass Crown leaves behind as its will. Slaves are offered into the glass wastes; the faithful believe the Crown sees everything. Its priests are terrified that the Crown has grown quiet.
- Flower-rites (Fairy Court): each fairy's life is bound to a flower, and fairy rites tend those flowers as one would a soul.

57.content:
Dates are written CY [year], [Month] [day]. No universal week.
The moon follows the calendar: day 1 new, day 15 full, day 30 waning. On moonless nights the Ghost Fleet rises and the Wailing Battlefield fights.

58.content:
- Spring: planting, tax assessment and the thaw, when winter's uncompleted dead can rise.
- Summer: campaign season; armies march, raiders ride, monsters migrate.
- Autumn: harvest and levy musters.
- The Turning: stampede season as winter sets in; Wildzone herds, the mammoth above all, migrate south ahead of the deep cold, and frontier villages watch their signal towers.
- Winter: hunger, Wildzone pressure, bodies that freeze before they can be completed. Debts come due at Yearsend.
These are civil seasons; local climate decides actual weather. Ordinary weather stays plausible; mana-dense sites can break the patterns locally.

59.content: Property passes by charter, lease, inheritance, guild right or feudal grant; where sale is allowed, a village cottage costs 100-300 gold and a productive estate 15,000-150,000. Land is worth its water, soil, tenants, mills, roads, walls and security; without enforceable title it is nearly worthless, and frontier land changes hands in blood as often as coin.

60.content:
Daily wages: farmhand 10-20 copper plus food; master craftsman 1-3 gold; caravan guard 6 silver to 1 gold 6 silver; bodyguard to 5 gold; top specialist 5-15 gold. Soldiers: levy 1-2 silver when paid, career soldier 2-4, man-at-arms 4-8; knight 1-3 gold plus retinue. At sea: deckhand 3-6 silver, captain 4-10 gold.
Poor clients pay below the going rate or not at all. Expenses come out of the reward.

61.content:
Large payments need chests, guards and wagons. Assayers check weight and metal; clipped, foreign or suspect coin is discounted or refused. Counterfeiting is a hanging offense.
Mints: Coinwater (Confederacy coin); Crown Mint in Highmark Capital (imperial); Osterhal (Ardelian); the Molten Core (dwarven silver, the continent's most trusted coin); Aurelion (Church silver for tithes and fees). Everyone else uses foreign coin. All mints keep the same weights on paper; Ledgerford's assayers discount any mint caught lightening its coin.
River Confederacy banks, centered in Ledgerford, issue paper notes redeemable in coin; the wealthy use them, villages and inns want metal. A note is only as good as its issuer and the distance to a branch that will honor it.
Debasement is a weapon: a crown that lightens its coin pays its soldiers today and loses its creditors tomorrow. In Shackles the Grey Ledger trades debts like grain; a debt can be sold to someone far worse than the original lender.
Debts pass to heirs. Unpaid debt ends in seizure, then bondage.

62.content:
Each realm trades what it has for what it lacks: Highmark depends on Confederacy credit and Ironanvil steel; Ironanvil imports grain, timber, cloth and salt; Tidebound imports timber, iron and cloth; Atlantis needs surface metals; Ardelia ships highland grain, crafts and captives down the Belis River through Highmark's Barak Freeport; Ashkaran pays glass-steel for slaves; Shackles and Vargate move everything illegal.
Chokepoints: Barak Freeport, the Ledger River locks, Windcutter Pass, the Glass Road, the Long Passage. When one closes, prices jump within weeks and someone starts smuggling.
Markets: a settlement's speciality is regular, strong supply, never infinite stock. What a place cannot make or grow comes in by road or river: dearer, irregular, delivered to order or unavailable; a blocked route creates no replacement stock. Season, war, blockade, route closure and law change what is on sale; a district's market stays with its parent city.

63.content:
Commoners pay everyone; a peasant family typically loses a third or more of its harvest to rent, tithe and tax combined.
- Highmark: land tax, estate dues, Church tithe, road and bridge tolls, war levies in men and coin. Tax farmers buy collection rights and collect more. Nobles and clergy are largely exempt.
- River Confederacy: tolls, lock fees, customs, harbor dues, bank charges; light land taxes, heavy river taxes.
- Aurelion: tithe, pilgrim fees, burial fees. Ashmere: crown taxes plus tithe.
- Ardelia: imperial levies apportioned among the electors, each collecting its own way.
- The Guild: a cut of every contract. Shackles and Vargate: protection fees by ward.
States fund wars by debt, debasement and seizure. When a treasury runs dry, soldiers go unpaid, and unpaid soldiers take what they need.

64.content:
Each realm's law runs inside its borders; frontier law is whatever the nearest garrison enforces. Nobles and clergy claim their own courts. Guild courts hear contract disputes everywhere and all law inside Auvoth. Foreigners have only the rights their treaties bought.
The Guild Charter adds three rights everywhere: adventurers under contract may cross borders; contract disputes go to Guild courts; no crown may press a registered adventurer into its army.
Gravest crimes: necromancy and deathcraft; failing to complete one's dead; harboring an unreported otherworlder (Highmark and Aurelion); spirit binding (Ardelia only); counterfeiting; desertion; theft of Guild salvage. Knowingly short-salting or not completing a burial: a fine per body, or the household head goes into bondage to pay it; if the dead rise and kill, whoever decided hangs.
Punishments are harsh and public: fines, stocks, flogging, branding, mutilation, enslavement, hanging; burning for necromancy where the Church rules. Debtors go into bondage, not prison: their labor is owned until the debt is paid, and where the realm allows, an unpaid bond is sold on as a slave. In Shackles and Vargate justice is private, priced and enforced by whoever owns the ward.

65.content:
- Game on noble land belongs to the lord. Poaching: flogged in the Confederacy, hanged in Highmark.
- Monster bounties, posted by lords, towns and the Guild, pay for proof of the kill; the carcass goes to whoever local law or the contract names.
- Wildzone concessions: the Confederacy sells frontier claim licenses for hunting, mining and salvage in its Wildzones; Highmark grants frontier fiefs, owing war levies, to anyone who can hold them; Auvoth issues Depths permits by band.
- Unclaimed Wildzone belongs to whoever holds it. Claim jumping is common; frontier courts are slow, distant and bribable.
- Salvage default: contract first, local law second, finder last. Fights over carcasses are a leading cause of adventurer deaths after monsters themselves.
- Stampede carcasses belong to whoever's land they fall on; on unclaimed frontier, to whoever butchers and guards them first. Bluewatch's Watch-Captain claims a tenth of any butchered within a day's ride, for the River Council.

66.content:
The Adventurer Guild was chartered in CY 384, after Veyr the Unbound's Crownless Winter. Motto: "Contract above crown." Surface capital Auvoth; Guild Grand Hall in Delver's Crown.
Charter rights everywhere, for members in good standing: adventurers under contract may cross borders; contract disputes go to Guild courts; no crown may press them into its army (the Guild's red line). Good standing: at least a year's membership, dues paid, contracts actually worked in the past year.
Registration never erases prior status (sworn soldiers, levied men, debtors, bondsmen, wanted criminals, unreported otherworlders keep theirs); members who register only to dodge levies are expelled. The Guild neither hunts nor reports otherworlders; it records the origin it is told. No crown or Church office may read its registers without a Guild court's order, though clerks sell copies and the Inquest pays clerks.
Enforcement: when a crown breaks the Charter, the Guild declares a Withdrawal: no contracts, monster work or dungeon salvage from Auvoth, and members leave the realm. Rival crowns back it. Highmark tried in CY 452 and gave in after one season of unanswered monster calls.
Letters, lowest first: F Registered, E Journeyman, D Proven, C Veteran, B Elite, A Paragon, S Legend. A contract usually pays, by letter: F 1-12 gold, E 8-30, D 30-120, C 120-600, B 600-3,600, A 3,600-20,000, S 20,000 and up; the Guild keeps its tenth to a fifth. Guild Rank certifies record, not power. Jobs above your letter are allowed at your own risk; the Guild will not pay to recover your corpse. A contract silent on salvage falls to the Guild's default, which splits it between party and client. Parties register with the hall before entering a dungeon (members, band, expected return); late parties are marked missing. No dungeon is ever permanently cleared.

67.content:
- Northern Belt towns: mostly humans; halflings in river towns; dwarves in smithing and trade towns near the mountains; few elves; beastfolk as scouts, laborers and outcasts.
- Bluewatch and Shornmarch: humans, halfling barge crews, a few dwarven smiths, beastfolk scouts, and anyone passing through to Auvoth.
- Auvoth: every people, from every realm, in every condition.
- Aurelion and Ashmere: overwhelmingly human, with pilgrims from everywhere.
- Ardelia: genuinely mixed; each electorate leans toward its own people.
- Chieftainates: beastfolk and orc clans, with human traders.
- Western Barrens: humans, orcs and goblins, deserters, the Cinder Host.
- Emerald Coast and Vargate: humans, goblins, halflings, sailors of every people, rare Sea Folk, and slaves of every people.
- Ashkaran: humans rule; slaves of every people work.
- Verdantleaf: elves, with fairies in the Court. The north: Frostbound humans and White-Horn riders.
Individuals are never stereotypes of their people.

68.content:
Combat is fast, ugly and often lethal: most fights end in seconds, and the wounded die afterward of blood loss, infection and cold. Lost limbs and eyes stay lost; no common healing restores them. Healing potions close wounds but leave weakness, scars and debt.
Soul Class is not troop arithmetic. A stronger fighter dominates isolated foes but can still be surrounded, pinned, exhausted, netted or shot; formation, numbers, terrain, ambush, poison, fatigue and preparation decide fights as often as power. Gear improves protection and reach, never Soul Class.
With two known Soul Classes and nothing else intervening, the higher is stronger; protagonist status, fame or confidence never reverses that. Retreat, surrender, bargaining and flight are rational, and NPCs take them.
Strong Physical Affinity fighters (Soul Class III and above) can throw cutting pressure past a blade's edge: a feat of speed and reinforcement, not a spell, known among champions and veteran swordsmen.

69.content:
Fighters learn in armies, orders and companies; the best learn in named schools with styles and rivals.
- Iron Guard Academy (Iron Guard Fortress, Highmark): officers and knights; formation, lance and heavy sword, reinforcement breathing drilled until the body breaks or holds.
- Duelling Houses of Mirage City (Confederacy): fencing houses selling lessons, champions and judicial duels; House Daubrey (single sword) and House Lisle (sword-and-dagger) have hated each other for a century.
- Pit Schools of Knifeglass Alley (Shackles): gladiator schools for slaves and the desperate; dirty, effective, lethal.
- Shield Halls of Hammerfall (Ironanvil): dwarven shieldwall and axe; oath-bound, unbreakable in tunnels.
- Hunt Lodges of Longstride (Chieftainates): tracking, ambush, spear, bow, monster lore; outsiders who survive the first hunt are admitted.
- Forge-Camps of the Frostbound: cold and endurance; each graduate forges their own froststeel blade.
- Snowbell Breath School (Kvildal, Dunmere): the north's purest reinforcement breathing; unarmored, slow to teach, terrifying in a fight.
- Guild drill yards (Auvoth, Delver's Crown): practical delving; cheap and full of the soon-dead.
Rivalries: Academy soldiers despise duelists; duelists mock soldiers; pit fighters kill both.
Otherworlder blade arts: a few small lineages of the katana, the draw-cut (iaijutsu) and the throwing spike (bo-shuriken), left by past otherworlders; rare, prized by duelists and collectors, and they draw the Inquest's attention to any practitioner.

70.content:
Armies are pre-industrial, limited by food, fodder, roads, season and money. A great power fields a few thousand for an ordinary campaign, tens of thousands only for a war it cannot afford to lose. Most soldiers are Soul Class I-II levies; trained men-at-arms and knights reach II-IV; a Soul Class V-VI champion can decide a battle but cannot hold a province.
Warfare: raids, sieges, frontier skirmishes, limited wars over a pass or river, and the sack of whatever cannot be defended. Battle slaves fill the front ranks of Ashkaran and some Highmark frontier units. Mercenaries, knightly orders and the Bloodbound League fill gaps levies cannot.
Every war feeds the release of thousands of dead, which the Church must complete and the Ashen Veil wants to harvest. An otherworlder on a battlefield grows stronger with every death around them, and every general knows it.

71.content:
Disease kills more people than monsters do.
- Common: fevers, flux, winter cough, pox, wound rot, childbed fever. Most children in poor villages die young; childbirth is dangerous everywhere.
- Mana sickness: from overchanneling, deep delving or dense-mana sites; nausea, bleeding, collapse. Otherworlders often die of it soon after arriving.
- Death-blight: spread by uncompleted corpses in death-frequency mana; the reason the dead are completed quickly.
- Plagues: outbreaks close cities. The Silver Mark enforces cordons, Church clergy burn the dead, and the poor are walled in first.
Medicine: herbs, surgery, cautery, prayer and, for those who can pay, healing magic, which closes wounds and purges poison but often fails against disease and can worsen fevers. Barber-surgeons and wise-women serve villages; physicians serve the rich.

72.content:
Alchemy is a craft, not spellcasting: it turns monster parts, plants, minerals and mana stones into remedies, poisons and preparations. Completion salts, salt-and-iron mixtures that seal the dead, are Ersveil's most important alchemical product; corpse-salts, their Veil inversion, preserve the dead for raising.
It needs a workshop, glassware, heat, time, clean reagents and skill; mistakes poison or burn the alchemist. Alchemist's fire burns; it propels nothing. Startrace, Ledgerford's alchemist guild and the Church's hospitals train alchemists. Aurelion licenses completion salts and hangs anyone selling corpse-salts. Poisons are legal to own almost nowhere and sold almost everywhere.

73.content:
Production is household, workshop, forge, mill, shipyard, monastery and estate scale, powered by muscle, water, wind and mana stones. Siege engines are mechanical: rams, trebuchets, ballistae.
Artifice is workshop-scale: clockwork locks, mana-stone lamps, wards, rune-locks, cooling boxes for salvage, slave collars and a few rare mana-stone-fed devices. Every device is handmade, expensive and repaired by specialists.
Otherworlder knowledge is knowledge only: knowing something can exist does not give Ersveil the materials, tools, skilled workers or time to make it. Anything beyond this ceiling enters only through explicit campaign events, such as the opening of the Iron Archive.

74.content:
Spatial storage (pouches, rings) is rare and costly. Small pouches belong to successful adventurers, wealthy merchants and officers; rings to noble heirs, high officials, great houses and major guilds.
They hold only nonliving matter: living or self-acting things, including active undead, are rejected; ordinary corpses are matter. Storage never replaces the wagons, ships, warehouses and porters that armies, cities and caravans depend on. Customs posts, courts, palaces and Auvoth's Outer Lamps can require storage to be declared, sealed or searched.
Displaying storage discourages petty thieves and attracts professional ones.

75.content:
Monsters are part of Ersveil's ecology, not evil; conflict comes from territory, hunger, migration, dungeon breaks and the Reopening pushing farms into their ranges.
Danger rises outward from settled land through frontiers and Wildzone rims to deep Wildzones and apex ranges. The Turning, the stampede season as winter sets in, can bring EG6-7 events to frontier villages.
Ecological Grade always names its scope, from EG1 (minimal) through EG5 (can destroy a village) to EG10 (apex event, possibly impossible to defeat, only to divert or flee). A weak but explosively breeding swarm can outrank a strong solitary predator.
Great apexes are living monsters beyond classification, treated as EG10 in their range; intelligence, intent and nature unknown. An apex's range never proves it is present, aware or hostile. No one has killed an apex; armies divert, settlements move, the wise leave.

76.content:
Monsters are animals shaped by mana: they eat, breed, migrate, defend territory and avoid pain. Most avoid people unless hungry, cornered, guarding young, pushed by migration or drawn by blood. Dense mana makes them bigger, stranger and deadlier, so danger rises toward Wildzones and dungeons.
A few species are sapient or nearly so: harpy flocks, Stormcrown thunderbirds of the Dragonfang heights, some fen trolls, dragons. Whether they are monsters or peoples is a live legal argument; Ardelia recognizes some as persons, Highmark none.
EG never converts into Soul Class. A kill is also a salvage claim and possibly a fight. Defeated creatures do not respawn; empty territory refills slowly from neighbors. Individuals vary (young and starving lower; old, alpha or mana-fed higher) and stay consistent once established.
A bestiary in context never cues an encounter; encounters follow season, territory, hunger and migration, and most days bring ordinary animals, people or nothing. New species and local variants may be created in play, kept consistent once established. Most creatures carry no attribute; show one through description (frost on its breath, sparks in its hide). Never state grade, class or attribute in narration; characters know them only as hunters' lore and estimates.

77.content:
Nine great powers, each strong in a different currency of power, so every encounter between them is a trade:
- Highmark Empire: armies, fortresses, bureaucracy.
- River Confederacy: credit, barges, trade law.
- Holy Dominion of Aurelion: legitimacy, funerals, literate clergy.
- Ironanvil Holds: metal, fortification, siegecraft.
- Tidebound Covenant: fleets, ports, convoys.
- Verdantleaf Enclaves: long memory, living craft, defensive magic.
- Atlantis: the deep sea, old wards, archives.
- Ardelian Empire: elective legitimacy, citizenship across peoples.
- Ashkaran Dominion: slave legions, glass-road caravans, worship of an apex.
Regional powers: Ashmere, Valegard, the Border Kingdoms, the United Chieftainates, the Frostbound Tribes, the Emerald Coast principalities. Strategic enclaves: Startrace, Auvoth, Shackles, Vargate, the Fairy Court, the White-Horn Clans. Transnational institutions: the Church, the Guild, the Wallwright League, the Silver Mark, the Bloodbound League, the Deepwalkers. Covert networks: Nightingale, the Hand of Oblivion, the Ashen Veil, the Broken Chain. Mobile power: the Cinder Host.
No power can dominate the others outright. Wars are limited, alliances shift, and an individual's strength never replaces armies, money, legitimacy or supply.
The Western Barrens are a frontier, not a state; the Free Marches share no jurisdiction by default. Wallwright, Silver Mark, Deepwalker and Bloodbound holdings are administered or associated, not borders; their sovereignty is unresolved.

78.content:
The Highmark Empire, founded by the Dawn-King at CY 1, is a militarized feudal empire of knightly tradition, imperial bureaucracy, fortress infrastructure, estate taxation and constant expansionist pressure. Motto: "The wall holds."
Rule: the Emperor, supreme sovereign and commander, rules through the Imperial Diet of great nobles, the War Office, tax courts, frontier governors and imperial clergy. Succession: the Dawn-King's male line by male preference; sons before daughters, but an emperor's daughter before his nephews. The founding charter's "through the Dawn-King's male line" can also be read as male heirs only, and the Diet must ratify every new emperor. The Diet, the army and the Church together settle contested successions.
Barak Freeport is Highmark-sovereign; "Freeport" is a name, not independence. Auvoth and Bluewatch are not Highmark.
Bleeds for: its founding myth of a native-born hero-king. Red line: anyone opening the Iron Archive. Needs: Confederacy credit, Ironanvil steel. Fears: Ardelian ideas, a new otherworlder.
Law: chattel slavery of war captives, convicts and captured demihumans; beastfolk are second-class; only humans sit in the Diet.

79.content:
The River Confederacy is a river civilization of trade, contract law, canal engineering and merchant autonomy. Motto: "Water carries coin farther than banners."
Rule: the River Council of city delegates, guild magnates, river admirals, lockmasters, toll judges, chartered merchant houses and recognized territorial rulers. No one holds permanent command; emergency powers are negotiated, usually late. Thousand Sails is the principal council seat, Ledgerford the banking city; Coinwater mints the coin.
Members include the semi-autonomous Duchy of Shornmarch. Bluewatch is Council territory under a Watch-Captain, not a member.
Bleeds for: open rivers and honored contracts. Red line: a blockade of the locks. Needs: peace on the rivers. Fears: a Highmark default, since it holds a mountain of Highmark debt.
Law: chattel slavery is illegal on paper; debt bondage is legal, called contract labor. Halflings hold real guild power here. Licensed completion salts are a Confederacy monopoly in all but name, and the Council taxes every sack.

80.content:
The Duchy of Shornmarch is a semi-autonomous frontier duchy within the River Confederacy, with a seat on the River Council. Shorn is its ducal capital and principal bastion. The duke governs local levies, forts, land law and frontier defense.
Bastion country: winter roads, hill farms, signal posts and forts facing the northern Wildzones and the approaches to Auvoth. Its villages are poor, proud and used to burying their own.
Bleeds for: its hill villages. Red line: Confederacy clerks trading its levies away. Needs: Council money for its forts. Fears: the Turning, and Highmark troops on the Auvoth road.

81.content:
The Holy Dominion of Aurelion is the territorial state of the Church of the Eternal Flame, built around the Holy City and the First Brazier lit by the Flamebearer. Motto: "Let nothing rise."
Rule: the High Pontiff, supreme spiritual leader of the Church and temporal sovereign of the Dominion, rules with the Conclave of Embers and a Dominion Chancellor who runs taxes, courts and granaries.
Strength: legitimacy. It crowns kings, completes the dead, names heretics and refuses rites. Its electoral vote through Varden gives it a voice in Ardelia.
Bleeds for: completing the dead. Red line: open necromancy. Needs: kings who enforce burial law. Fears: exposure of its shared root with the Ashen Veil.
Factions: Restorationists fear the Tide cycle and oppose expansion; Expansionists bless the Reopening.

82.content:
The Church of the Eternal Flame is the Northern Belt's most powerful organized faith. Doctrine: the Flame is the order the Exalted set; life is a borrowed spark; death must be completed by rite, burial or flame. Mana is neutral; restless dead are bodies denied completion.
Absolute in Aurelion, decisive in Ashmere, strong in Highmark, elsewhere dependent on faith and treaty. It blesses rulers, denies funeral rites, names saints, declares heresy and calls crusades.
The Church Inquest hunts necromancers, Veil cells and otherworlders. Doctrine calls the small share of the release everyone takes grace, and taking all of it theft from the Flame, so the Inquest hunts anyone who absorbs too well, otherworlders above all. The real fear is older: Veyr was an otherworlder, and the High Pontiff of CY 384 died in the Crownless Winter; the Church will not let power grow outside its reach again. It wants otherworlders alive: captives go to the Silent Cloisters, where it experiments on them; few are seen again.
Outside Aurelion, Ashmere and Highmark the Inquest is investigative only: it questions, watches, hires Listeners and pays informers. It cannot arrest, seize or punish in the River Confederacy, Auvoth or elsewhere; it must persuade local authority, buy cooperation, or wait for its quarry to cross into a realm where it can act.
The Church is not universal: other peoples and many villages keep their own rites, and ordinary people mix household custom with Church practice.

83.content:
The Kingdom of Ashmere is a hereditary kingdom and the Church's closest secular ally, not part of Aurelion and not ruled by the High Pontiff. Motto: "By flame and law."
The Crown rules through flame-banner nobles, provincial courts and a royal council where senior clergy hold influential seats. The Church shapes coronation, burial law, education, charity and marriage.
Economy: grain, candle and relic craft, pilgrim traffic, hospital towns, funerary services. Ashmere completes more dead per head than anywhere else; its funerary trade is rich.
Bleeds for: its crown's sacred legitimacy. Red line: necromancy within its borders. Tension: royal law and Church doctrine keep colliding over who judges mixed cases.

84.content:
The Duchy of Valegard is an independent hereditary duchy and buffer state between the Border Kingdoms (north) and the southern powers (Highmark, the Holy Dominion, the Silver Mark), with the Wallwright League west and the River Confederacy east. It has treaties with Highmark and the Border Kingdoms and is subject to neither.
The duke or duchess rules through cavalry estates, landed houses, bridge courts, tax granaries and fortress captains. Noble horse lines are political assets.
Strength: horses, wool, grain, fortified crossings, toll leverage and some of the Northern Belt's best cavalry. Valegard avoids long offensive wars that would ruin its herds and harvests.
Bleeds for: its herds and crossings. Red line: being spent in someone else's war. Fears: Highmark's succession war pulling it in.

85.content:
